raw_comment:
The regions with the greatest loss in bird population seem to follow a common pattern of the jet stream when cold arctic air dips down into the central plains area of US, especially during the winter. Bye-Bye Birdie

I notice that most places have at least a decrease of almost 20% in bird population, with grassland being the highest. This is most likely due to deforestation and populating new areas. Our effect against the environment can lead us to endanger American birds. This can also mean other animals too. For example, wild buffalo went from the millions into just over 1000. It will be sad if we lose an American animal.

I wonder if there are ways to reverse this effect on the bird population. Do we have to regrow some forest? What are some possible solutions?

Bird Population within environments lowering in many cases!
I notice that since 1970 the bird population in many areas has lowered especially in the grasslands which according to the graph has decreased by about 50%.  I also notice that while the grasslands, boreal forest, western forests, tundra, generalist, forest generalist, eastern forests, arid lands, and coast have all decreased in bird population, the wetlands are still increasing by about 15% as of 2010.  I wonder if the bird population has began to get better, or if the bird population is continuing to lower at a detrimental rate, and if so are the wetlands still increasing in the bird population?

I notice that wetlands are the only one with an increase in population, while grasslands have the largest decrease in population.
I wonder if the reason of these changes are because of the resources we take from these regions. We humans don't take many, if any, resources from the wetlands, but most of our resources come from the Grasslands.
Losing Birds, Gaining Resources

raw_comment:
I notice in this graph that the bird population changed the most in the grasslands, with a negative change of 53%. Also, it’s showing where the biomes are, and it seems to me that all the central biomes (on land) lost the most, with biomes to the edges like wetlands losing less or even gaining.
I wonder:
Why did wetlands manage to gain birds while all others lost them?
Since the boreal forests have more area but lost a less percentage, did they lose more birds in total than the grasslands?
How many birds were lost in total?
Title: 
“Who dives faster: bird populations or peregrine falcons? Surprisingly, it might be birds.”

What I noticed - 

I noticed that in the grasslands, boreal forests, western forests, tundra, generalist, forest generalist, eastern forests, arid lands, and coasts the bird population has greatly decreased. Mainly in the grasslands where it has decreased by over 50%. The only place the bird population has increased is in the wetlands where it has increased by a little over 10%.

What I wondered - 

I wonder why the bird population has gone down everywhere except for the wetlands. I wonder if it is because there are less humans living in the wetlands so there are less people killing the birds. Or maybe is it because of a series of bad genetic mutations in those habitats.

1) Despite Canada appearing to be widely proactive in their fight against climate change, the decline in population of birds exists in their country as well. This means that their legislators are not keeping up with the impact of mass extinction as well.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
- A **composite visualization** combining:
  - a **thematic habitat map** of North America,
  - a **horizontal bar chart** showing percent change since 1970 by breeding habitat,
  - a **multi-series line chart** showing cumulative net loss over time.

2. **Layout techniques**  
- **Multiple coordinated views**: map on the left, summary bar chart at top right, time-series line chart at bottom right.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- The line chart uses **multiple colored lines** (not stacked).
- The map uses **color-filled regions** to show habitat categories.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Breeding habitat | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue on map regions; color/hue of bars; color/hue of lines; text labels |
| Geographic region / habitat area location | Spatial | Position on map |
| Bird population change since 1970 (%) | Quantitative | Horizontal position / bar length in the bar chart |
| Year (1970, ’80, ’90, 2000, ’10) | Temporal | Position on x-axis in the line chart |
| Net loss of birds (millions) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis in the line chart |
| Country/continent basemap (North America) | Spatial/reference | Background map outlines |

1. **Chart type**  
- A **composite visualization** combining:
  - a **thematic habitat map** of North America,
  - a **horizontal bar chart** showing percent change since 1970 by breeding habitat,
  - a **multi-series line chart** showing cumulative net loss over time.

2. **Layout techniques**  
- **Multiple coordinated views**: map on the left, summary bar chart at top right, time-series line chart at bottom right.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- The line chart uses **multiple colored lines** (not stacked).
- The map uses **color-filled regions** to show habitat categories.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Breeding habitat | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue on map regions; color/hue of bars; color/hue of lines; text labels |
| Geographic region / habitat area location | Spatial | Position on map |
| Bird population change since 1970 (%) | Quantitative | Horizontal position / bar length in the bar chart |
| Year (1970, ’80, ’90, 2000, ’10) | Temporal | Position on x-axis in the line chart |
| Net loss of birds (millions) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis in the line chart |
| Country/continent basemap (North America) | Spatial/reference | Background map outlines |

raw_comment:
Headline: Not Waking Up to the Birds Chirping.

I notice that toward the late 80s and early 90s the bird population began to decline quite quickly. This may be because of the introduction of pesticides that destroyed the bird population and the expansion of companies across America. In addition, the west coast has a heavy mix of dry land and western forest, but there is a difference in bird population decline between the two. 

I wonder why the coast had a decrease in their bird population, but the wetlands had an increase? Does water play a role in the increase & decrease of bird populations?

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph shows how the North America bird population is changing by habitat.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and  "What's going on in this graph?"  

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas about the graph. 

On Thursday afternoon, we’ll reveal the article that included this graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

The next “What’s Going On in This Graph?” will be released tomorrow -- Thursday, January 16, with moderation on Wednesday, January 22.  The topic – “water stress,” that is, population and the availability of water around the world.  Stay tuned.

raw_comment: This graph shows the changes in bird population since 1970 based on different regions and breeding areas. In most regions, the number of birds has gone down drastically. The largest decrease was in the Grasslands region, where the population has gone down over 50%. Other large decreases include the Boreal Forests, Western Forests, and the Tundra. Unlike in other regions, the percentage of birds in the wetlands has increased by a little over 10%. I wonder why most bird populations have decreased and why populations in the wetlands have increased. I also wonder what can be done to stop this increase. One possible title could be "Dying Bird Populations."

raw_comment:
1.  I wonder what is causing such a huge decline in bird population. Upon doing some research, I found that the leading factors behind their decline are collisions with glass, pesticides, hunting by domestic cats, and by human hunters. This means that out of these 4 leading factors, 3 of the cause are inflicted by humans. Not only are humans contaminating the environment, but some are also killing birds as a sport. People should be more considerate of the repercussions of  their actions when it comes to these poor defenseless (against humans) animals.
2. What many people may also not consider is that the decline of bird population is also dangerous for plants. Due to their constant travel, birds serve as pollinators and they spread seeds. If birds go extinct, plants would struggle to reproduce in other areas and eventually a great majority of nature would die off. Considering that bees (which are also in danger) also help to pollinate and promote plant growth, there won't be as many options left for plants to disperse. 
3. I wonder if people consider that instead of using pesticide and destroying the habitats of birds, they could take car of the habitats and let nature take its course. Birds can get rid of insects that are considered pests; it's in their nature. So by aiding the conservation of these habits, they will promote a more natural pesticide: birds.

- A **composite visualization** combining:
  - a **thematic habitat map** of North America,
  - a **horizontal bar chart** showing percent change since 1970 by breeding habitat,
  - a **multi-series line chart** showing cumulative net loss over time.

2. **Layout techniques**  
- **Multiple coordinated views**: map on the left, summary bar chart at top right, time-series line chart at bottom right.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- The line chart uses **multiple colored lines** (not stacked).
- The map uses **color-filled regions** to show habitat categories.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Breeding habitat | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue on map regions; color/hue of bars; color/hue of lines; text labels |
| Geographic region / habitat area location | Spatial | Position on map |
| Bird population change since 1970 (%) | Quantitative | Horizontal position / bar length in the bar chart |
| Year (1970, ’80, ’90, 2000, ’10) | Temporal | Position on x-axis in the line chart |
| Net loss of birds (millions) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis in the line chart |
| Country/continent basemap (North America) | Spatial/reference | Background map outlines |

raw_comment:
1. I researched and came to the conclusion that invasive species including human settlement is a huge factor to why bird population has decreased. I wonder if construction companies even consider the threats they may pose to the atmosphere and society before constructing?

2. I'm so stunned to see that the arid lands have had a stable population of birds compared to the drastic decrease of birds in the grasslands. I would imagine that since the arid lands tend to be more dry, they would have a decrease in bird population, but that doesn't seem to be the case.

3. To my surprise the wetlands is the place where the bird population migrates and there they are able to breed, nest and shelter. Also human settlement is not popular in the wetlands, instead the human race benefits from the wetlands mostly due to their natural products such as water. So because of the lack of human settlement in the wetlands, that might be the reason why they are thriving in a high percentage of bird population.

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that lands in higher terrain such as forests were more directly affected, perhaps because they are more susceptible to climate change's effects.

2. Boreal forests have a northern climate which is often colder than other forests such as the Eastern and Western forests, so this may suggest that the increase in global warming is more affecting the Boreal forests since the animal inhabitants of that region are accustomed to a cooler climate.

3. I wonder why the Western forests overlap with arid lands and grasslands and don't have the same climates.

1. I wonder why, despite the fact that California is on the Coast and has a large access to water, there was still a significant decrease in the bird population. 

2.  I wonder why, despite the fact that the Boreal forests occupy a larger land area, the grasslands still have a significantly greater negative change in the bird population. 

3. I wonder the true factors that would cause such a great loss of bird population in the past 48 years from 1970-2010 in all geographical locations.
